definition: Schelling's philosophy of nature that conceives nature not as a static mechanical system but as a self-organizing, dynamic, living process structured in an ascending series of potencies (Potenzen) containing polar oppositions; nature is visible spirit, spirit is invisible nature — the real and the ideal are two expressions of one absolute activity, beginning from the real rather than the ideal

definition: Schelling's mature identity philosophy (1801-1807) that posits the absolute as the indifference point of subject and object, real and ideal — the identity of thought and being is not achieved through synthesis but is the primordial ground from which the distinction between subject and object first emerges; breaking with the model of truth as correspondence, this philosophy holds that what is split in judgment must already be the same
connective_patterns: the absolute as indifference point of subject and object

definition: Dynamic levels or grades of reality through which the absolute articulates itself as a series of increasingly complex forms and forces — in Naturphilosophie the potencies are matter (equilibrium of expansive and contractive forces), light (magnetism, electricity, chemical action), and organism (reproduction, irritability, sensibility); each potency contains within itself a polar opposition that drives the dialectical ascent

definition: The abyssal, pre-rational ground of all existence — a pure indifference or will that precedes the distinction between ground (Grund) and existence (Existenz), between identity and difference; drawing on Jakob Boehme's mystical theology, the Ungrund names the dark, spontaneous, freely acting source that cannot be rationalized by any logical system, including Hegel's

definition: The unconditioned unity of real and ideal, nature and spirit, subject and object — not an abstract identity but a living, self-differentiating totality; for the later Schelling, the true absolute is not Hegel's logical Idea but a ground that is itself an unground (Ungrund), a pure indifference that precedes the very distinction between identity and difference

definition: The central theme of Schelling's 1809 Freiheitsschrift — freedom is not mere absence of constraint but the capacity for good and evil rooted in the dark ground (Grund) of existence; evil is not privation but a positive possibility arising from the inversion of ground and existence, making human freedom genuinely consequential rather than merely formal

definition: The dark, irrational, longing element within God and within human beings — ground (Grund) is distinguished from existence (Existenz) as that which precedes and enables it; the ground is the will that yearns for existence but which, in human beings, can be inverted to become the source of evil when it asserts itself independently of the light of existence

definition: Not dead mechanism but the visible face of spirit — nature is a self-organizing, productive process (natura naturans) that evolves through polar tensions and potencies toward the emergence of consciousness; Schelling's nature is the unconscious productivity that precedes and underlies the conscious activity of spirit, making nature and spirit aspects of one absolute process

definition: The invisible counterpart of nature — spirit (Geist) is nature become conscious of itself, the ideal pole of the absolute's self-differentiation; whereas nature is the unconscious productivity that builds toward consciousness, spirit is the conscious reflection that recognizes nature as its own objective expression, completing the circle of absolute identity

definition: The dynamic principle of opposition within unity that drives the development of nature and spirit through the potencies — every level of reality exhibits a polar tension between contractive and expansive forces (e.g., magnetism, electricity, chemical affinity) whose interplay generates the ascending series of natural forms and the eventual emergence of consciousness

definition: Schelling's late philosophical program that begins from actual existence rather than from logical possibility — positive philosophy confronts what pure reason cannot deduce: the sheer fact that something exists; it addresses existence through mythology, revelation, and the free act of the absolute, going beyond the merely logical construction of negative philosophy to encounter the real in its irreducible actuality
